column3: The same recompense formula for doers of good provides a useful positive counterpart to the focus's negative recompense.
It nearly repeats the focus's pairing of recompense with disbelief and the ungrateful person, while specifying Hell.
A second generic formula for rewarding good-doers adds little after the first positive counterpart.
Noah's deliverance as recompense for one denied connects recognition or rejection to a fitting divine response.
Another generic reward for good-doers is redundant after the earlier examples.
It joins disbelief with severe punishment and frames the source of all earthly blessing as the One disbelieved in.
It explicitly states Hell as their recompense because they disbelieved in and mocked God's signs.
Disbelief after granted authority and security clarifies ingratitude as misusing a bestowed blessing.
A concrete restriction imposed as recompense for wrongdoing shows that recompense can be historically particular.
Their disbelief is followed by a future recognition of its consequence, but it adds little to the repayment theme.
The destruction of Aad is explicitly called recompense for criminals, supplying a historical punitive instance.
It gives the general principle of a full recompense corresponding to a person's striving.
The opening of David's dispute narrative does not clarify disbelief, ingratitude, or recompense.
Turning away and disbelieving identifies the culpable response but does not add a distinct account of recompense.
The introduction to Moses' story has no substantive relation to the focus.
It warns disbelievers of their promised day, a broad consequence already represented more specifically.
It links the curse on disbelievers to persistent disobedience and transgression, adding a historical moral cause.
Disbelief in the signs and its evil outcome is a broad parallel without the focus's repayment language.
The exception for those who pray does not interpret the focus's ungratefulness or recompense.
The rebuke of human ingratitude, in a creation-and-provision sequence, directly develops the focus's kafur character.
The image of unhearing disbelievers gives a general account of rejection but not its recompense.
Persistent denial is a broad counterpart to the focus's disbelief with no new consequence.
Its correction of fatalistic speech in battle does not materially clarify the focus.
Reward for what people did supplies only a general positive statement of recompense.
Disbelief in God's signs, disobedience, and transgression are tied to humiliation and wrath, a concrete punitive pattern.
The statement that disbelievers remain in denial adds little beyond earlier direct disbelief passages.
Rewarding the patient with success provides a distinct positive counterpart to punishment for unbelief.
Pharaoh's charge of ingratitude concerns his political claim over Moses rather than the focus's divine repayment.
Another formula rewarding good-doers is redundant after earlier positive examples.
Disbelief in the Creator of the earth frames unbelief as refusing the source of the provision later described.
The repeated reward for good-doers adds no marginal clarification after the prior examples.
The direct command to give thanks and not disbelieve states the moral opposite of the focus's ungratefulness.
The description of a persistently ungrateful generation offers only a remote narrative parallel.
Withholding zakah and denying the Hereafter identifies a form of rejection, but not the focus's recompense.
Their plotting and its reversal do not materially explain disbelief as ungratefulness.
Hell as recompense for wrongful claims of divinity gives a specific punitive application of the formula.
The battlefield outcome for disbelievers does not clarify the focus's moral-recompense relation.
It depicts people enjoying rescue and provision while disbelieving in what God gave them, a close ingratitude parallel.
Mockery of successive prophets is too general to add beyond stronger rejection passages.
It makes clear that human disbelief does not diminish the self-sufficient and praiseworthy Giver.
It explicitly promises severe punishment and recompense according to the worst of the disbelievers' deeds.
Treachery and ingratitude are condemned together, but the verse adds no consequence or blessing setting.
Satanic promises and delusion do not directly clarify the focus.
The best reward for believers is only a broad positive counterpart to the focus.
The curse as recompense for apostasy is a punitive parallel, but less specific than earlier disbelief passages.
False intermediary worship is described as the way of a lying, ungrateful person, sharpening the focus's kufr.
It explicitly calls punishment of disbelievers their recompense, adding a concrete earthly instance.
The principle that goodness is repaid with goodness is a concise positive contrast to the focus's punishment of ingratitude.
Additional punishment for disbelievers who obstruct God's way develops graded recompense for compounded corruption.
The bare address to disbelievers does not add substantive clarification.
Return to God for just reward, with painful punishment for disbelief, gives the focus an eschatological frame.
The brothers' discussion of a legal penalty is not a useful divine-recompense parallel.
It explicitly identifies punishment as recompense for disbelief in God's signs and denial of resurrection.
It states that creation is ordered so every soul may be repaid for what it earned without injustice.
Reward for believers from divine bounty is a broad positive counterpart, already well represented.
Receiving a blessing, then forgetting God and associating partners, closely illustrates ungrateful disbelief and its fire outcome.
The recompense of wrongdoers with fire is a general punitive formula without the focus's disbelief theme.
The conditional conflict ruling uses a different context of punishment and adds no focused clarification.
Forgiveness and the best reward for believers provide only a remote positive contrast.
It links denial of the signs and the Hereafter to the nullification of deeds and recompense for what was done.
Belief followed by disbelief and sealed hearts is a general rejection pattern without a recompense detail.
Rewarding patience with paradise is a positive counterpart already covered by stronger recompense examples.
It connects the futile-world assumption of disbelievers to woe in the Fire, supplying a theological consequence.
Destroyed earlier generations who rejected clear messengers are explicitly described through God's recompense of criminals.
Disbelievers' eventual admission of truth before tasting punishment directly joins disbelief to its consequence.
Reward for believers' good deeds adds no marginal value after earlier positive parallels.
The promise to recompense the grateful directly contrasts with the focus's recompense of the ungrateful.
Wastefulness is tied to Satan's ingratitude, extending kufr into the misuse of bestowed resources.
It states that disbelievers are repaid only for their deeds, but repeats the general principle already established.
Every soul's recompense for its earnings, without injustice, clarifies the focus's implied fairness.
Within the same surah, commanded disbelief leads to remorse, punishment, and the statement that people are repaid for their deeds.
It rejects identity-based immunity and states that whoever does evil will be repaid for it.
God's oversight of every soul's earnings, contrasted with associating partners, grounds accountable disbelief.
Calling God a part through His servants is labeled manifest ingratitude, specifying a form of kufr.
The reward of repentant righteous people is a redundant positive counterpart.
Leaving final repayment to God offers a general accountability frame without the focus's ingratitude.
Denial of resurrection followed by disclosure of deeds is a broad disbelief-and-accountability parallel.
Human ingratitude despite life, death, and renewed life identifies a foundational form of the focus's kufr.
Enjoying worldly good while persisting in arrogance and transgression leads to humiliating punishment.
God's reward of charitable givers does not materially clarify punishment for ingratitude.
Refusal of forgiveness is tied to disbelief in God and His messenger, reinforcing the seriousness of the focus's kufr.
God's complete ownership and self-sufficiency show that disbelief harms the recipient of blessing, not God.
Following falsehood rather than truth explains disbelief broadly but adds no recompense or gratitude dimension.
Temporary worldly enjoyment followed by severe punishment because of disbelief closely contrasts apparent benefit with final recompense.
Selective belief and grave social wrongdoing receive worldly disgrace and greater final punishment, a concrete recompense case.
The formula of tasting eternal punishment for one's earnings is redundant after stronger direct repayment passages.
Fear and the Fire for associating disbelievers provide a broad punitive consequence only.
Rain is distributed as a reminder, yet most people respond only with ingratitude, directly connecting blessing and kufr.
God's comprehensive knowledge and future disclosure of deeds do not specifically develop the focus.
Innumerable divine favors are followed by the description of humanity as unjust and ungrateful, directly defining the focus's condition.
The closing question asks whether disbelievers have been repaid for what they did, a concise direct parallel.
Its recompense exactly corresponding to deeds gives a precise formulation of the fitting repayment asserted in the focus.
Disbelievers' disputation and worldly movement do not add beyond the established rejection-and-punishment pattern.
Those who mislead and follow them share enduring Fire as the recompense of wrongdoers.
Its distinction between Solomon and disbelieving devils in the magic narrative does not clarify the focus's repayment.
Rejecting the signs in arrogance brings exclusion from paradise and is explicitly called recompense for criminals.
The Companions of the Cave seeking refuge is unrelated to the focus's recompense for disbelief.
Another generic reward for good-doers adds no marginal value.
Its portrait and reward of believers does not clarify the focus beyond a distant contrast.
Rejecting and turning away from clear guidance is met with evil punishment, directly linking sustained disbelief to recompense.
The immediately preceding account gives Sabāʾ secure provision and commands gratitude, supplying the blessing that the focus's recompense answers.
Sabāʾ's turning away and the replacement of its fertile gardens are the immediate historical punishment summarized in the focus.
The command to David's household to work in gratitude, while few servants are grateful, supplies the same-surah positive counterpart.
It explicitly contrasts increased favor for gratitude with severe punishment for ingratitude.
Those who exchange God's favor for disbelief and lead their people to ruin provide a close blessing-to-punishment parallel.
People recognize God's favor and then deny it; the verse directly identifies most of them as disbelievers.
A secure, well-provisioned town that disbelieves in God's favors is made to taste hunger and fear, closely paralleling Sabāʾ's reversal.
Solomon calls divine bounty a test of gratitude or ingratitude and states that the ungrateful harm only themselves.
It makes gratitude beneficial to the grateful person and declares God self-sufficient when one is ungrateful.
God's freedom from human disbelief and approval of gratitude clarify why the focus's recompense addresses the recipient's response.
Humanity is shown the way as either grateful or ungrateful, giving a concise direct contrast central to the focus.
The rhetorical question of why God would punish those who are grateful and believe supplies a direct inverse of the focus.
Deliverance from land and sea distress followed by association illustrates rejection after an experienced divine rescue.
Settlement and provision on earth followed by little gratitude gives a broad antecedent pattern for the focus's ingratitude.
Rescue at sea followed by rebellion portrays received deliverance being answered with rejection.
The command to eat God's lawful provision and give thanks directly frames the grateful alternative to the focus's kufr.
People call on God in danger at sea, then turn away after rescue; it ends by calling the human ungrateful.
The gifts of hearing, sight, and hearts are followed by the rebuke that people give little thanks.
Those rescued at sea worship God sincerely, then associate partners after reaching land, a close reversal of gratitude.
People call on God in harm but associate partners after He lets them taste mercy, linking benefit to ungrateful rejection.
The reminder that God could make drinking water bitter ends by asking why people are not grateful.
The gift of hearing, sight, and hearts, followed by little gratitude, gives another concise provision-and-ingratitude parallel.
